idiom_name: Drools/KIE from Kotlin: DRL rules bound to Kotlin data-class facts
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no rule engine of its own; the JVM answer is Drools/KIE, and it works with Kotlin facts because data-class properties compile to JavaBean accessors that DRL patterns can bind. Rules stay in .drl files, facts are inserted into a KieSession, and consequences that change a fact must use modify()/update() (with setters, so the property must be a var) so the engine re-evaluates dependents. Keep one session per unit of work and let the KieContainer build the KieBase at startup.
pitfalls: modify()/setDiscount() needs a JavaBean setter, so immutable val properties cannot be updated by a consequence - use var properties, or insert a new fact and let the engine rematch.
A boolean property named isActive compiles to isActive() rather than getActive(), so DRL/JavaBean property resolution can bind a different name than Kotlin call sites use.
DRL resolves class and property names when the KieBase is built: renaming a Kotlin property breaks rules at build or first run, not in the IDE.

variants.name: Typed Kotlin rule list
variants.idiom_name: immutable rule list (when/then lambdas) folded over a data class
variants.implementation_notes: The Kotlin-native realization keeps rules as data without an engine: a list of Rule objects holding a predicate and a transition, evaluated by folding the fact through them. Immutable data classes with copy() make each step a pure transformation, so the rule set is trivially unit-testable and the outcome can be a sealed type matched exhaustively. Use it when rules are code and the decision must be refactor-safe; use Drools when rules are authored outside the codebase or must match across facts, which this variant cannot express.
pitfalls: Rules as lambdas are compiled: changing one needs a new build, which is exactly what a rule store outside the code avoids - do not sell this variant as business-editable.
Because copy() returns a new fact, later rules see earlier rules' results: that chaining must be intentional and documented, not accidental.
Nothing enforces determinism: overlapping conditions are order-dependent, so precedence has to be encoded in the list order or the rules made disjoint.
